tier_reason: Upgraded C to B: Martin Ankerl's well-known independent hashmap benchmark (2019 run, raw results in martinus/map_benchmark data/all.txt) timed eastl::hash_map directly against std::unordered_map with the same hash and shows EASTL faster in 56 of 63 rows (geomean 1.31x, derived from page data). Not A: the eastl adapter is gone from the suite's HEAD, the 2019 compiler version and flags are unconfirmed, and the CPU (i7-8700) comes from a search snippet; EASTL's own doc/Benchmarks.md (VC++ 7.1, no CPU, inexact flags) alone would be C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Independent (Martin Ankerl map_benchmark 2019 run, data/all.txt, medians of 10 runs per cell, std::unordered_map time divided by eastl::hash_map time with the same hash functor, derived from page data): with robin_hood::hash, random find 1.27-1.62x at 200 entries, 1.21-1.58x at 2,000 and 1.51-1.72x at 500,000 (0-100% success); 13-byte string find over 1M entries 1.48-1.59x and 100-byte string find 1.18-1.24x; random insert/erase 1.26-1.77x (4-24 bits, 50M cycles); string insert/erase 1.05-1.58x; reinsert 100M ints 1.31x, remove 1.14x; geomean 1.31x over 63 rows (1.31-1.42x across the five hashes tested), EASTL faster in 56 of 63. Slower: clear 100M ints 0.53x, destructor 0.39x, insert 100M ints 0.96x, iterate while adding/removing 0.96x/0.84x, distinct counting 0.80-0.85x at 5% and 100% distinct. First-party (EASTL doc/Benchmarks.md, 0.96.00, Win32 VC++ 7.1 Release against the Dinkumware stdext::hash_map; ratio = VC++ time / EASTL time): hash_map<uint32_t,TestObject> find 1.55x, insert 1.64x, operator[] 1.21x, count 2.51x, iteration 1.18x, erase val 1.54x, erase range 5.26x; hash_map<string,uint32_t> find 3.26x, find_as/char* 3.70x, insert 1.24x, operator[] 3.10x, count 3.77x, iteration 3.67x; slower clear 0.53x and 0.38x, erase pos 0.79x and 0.56x. Against STLport (same doc, Release) near parity: uint32 find 0.81x, insert 0.90x, operator[] 0.99x; string find 1.04x, insert 1.00x, find_as/char* 2.73x, iteration 1.90x.
corrections.baseline: std::unordered_map (directly in Ankerl's map_benchmark, Linux build); EASTL's own tables used the pre-standard stdext::hash_map of VC++ 7.1 (Dinkumware) and STLport's hash_map, and N2271 used GCC 4.1 libstdc++
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Ankerl map_benchmark: CMake Release; the current CMakeLists.txt sets -DNDEBUG -O3 -march=native, but the 2019 run's compiler version and flags are not confirmed (blog blocked). EASTL doc/Benchmarks.md: Microsoft Visual C++ 7.1 (version 1310), 'Full optimization. Inlining enabled' (exact flags not given), PPMalloc::GeneralAllocator. N2271: Windows column VC8 -Og -Oi -Ot -Oy -Ob2 -GF -Gy; Linux column GCC 4.1 -O3 with libstdc++.
corrections.hardware: Ankerl 2019 run: Intel i7-8700 at 3.2 GHz, one isolated core, frequency scaling disabled (search snippet only; blog blocked). EASTL doc/Benchmarks.md gives no CPU. N2271 lists Pentium 4 x86 (Windows and Linux columns), a 64-bit PowerPC console and a G5 PowerPC Mac, without exact models.
corrections.workload: Independent: Ankerl map_benchmark 2019 workloads (random find at 200, 2,000 and 500,000 entries with 0-100% success, random insert/erase at 4-24 bits for 50M cycles, string find and string insert/erase, 100M-int insert/reinsert/remove/clear, iteration while adding/removing, distinct counting), same hash functor for both maps, five hashes. First-party: stopwatch (CPU cycles) comparison of eastl::hash_map against the compiler-supplied hash map on 10,000 random pairs with keys drawn from [0,5000), for uint32_t->TestObject and string->uint32_t, timing insert, find, operator[], count, erase, iteration and clear.
corrections.caveats: Independent evidence: Martin Ankerl's 2019 hashmap benchmark (raw results in data/all.txt of github.com/martinus/map_benchmark, whose lineup of boost 1_65_1, emilib1, spp and eastl::hash_map matches the 2019 run) timed eastl::hash_map against std::unordered_map with the same hash functor; EASTL is faster in 56 of 63 workload rows (geomean 1.31x with robin_hood::hash, derived from page data) but loses on clear of 100M ints (0.53x), destruction (0.39-0.51x), iterate while removing (0.84x), 100% distinct counting (0.85x) and empty-map construct/destroy (about 0.03 s vs a std time of about 1e-7 s, i.e. std's was optimized away). The same data shows the chained, node-based EASTL map far behind flat maps: absl::flat_hash_map about 2.4x faster and robin_hood::unordered_flat_map about 2.9x faster (geomean, EASTL wins 0 of 63 rows against either), folly::F14ValueMap about 1.6x faster (EASTL wins 10 of 63); EASTL beats boost::unordered_map 1.65 by about 1.11x (all derived from page data). The 2019 blog page (martin.ankerl.com) is blocked here; its i7-8700 machine, isolated core and disabled frequency scaling come from a search snippet only, and the 2019 compiler version and flags are not confirmed (the current CMakeLists.txt sets -DNDEBUG -O3 -march=native). The eastl adapter is no longer in map_benchmark's src/maps at HEAD, the 2022 rerun dropped EASTL, and the 2019 overview calls EASTL 'a bit dated' (snippet). First-party tables: doc/Benchmarks.md (EASTL 0.96.00, Win32, Microsoft Visual C++ 7.1, PPMalloc allocator, no CPU, 'Full optimization. Inlining enabled' without exact flags, single stopwatch run in CPU cycles, no variance) compares against the pre-standard stdext::hash_map of the Dinkumware STL and STLport's hash_map, not std::unordered_map; against STLport in Release EASTL is near parity and slower on uint32 find (0.81x) and insert (0.90x). The 2007 WG21 paper N2271 (doc/EASTL-n2271.pdf, by EASTL's author) Linux column (Pentium 4, GCC 4.1 -O3, libstdc++) shows uint32-key find 0.76x, insert 0.91x, operator[] 1.37x and string-key find 0.75x, iteration 0.54x, insert 3.52x, operator[] 3.00x, so EASTL was slower than libstdc++ on find. The current benchmark/source/BenchmarkHash.cpp targets std::unordered_map (10,000 pairs, keys in [0,5000), FNV-1a string hash for both) but its results are not published, and the tables are cache-resident. The library-wide claim in doc/Design.md and doc/FAQ.md that 'EASTL is faster than all existing STL implementations' is not supported for this facility. hash_set has no separate numbers; the record covers hash_map.

notes: Numbers in the record match doc/Benchmarks.md's Win32.VC71.MS.Release table exactly (uint32 iteration 1.18x was omitted; added). Upgraded to B on Ankerl's third-party raw data, where eastl::hash_map beats std::unordered_map about 1.3x geomean but trails absl::flat_hash_map about 2.4x and robin_hood flat map about 2.9x and loses on clear/destroy. Shortcomings: 20-year-old first-party tables against pre-standard hash_map, near parity with STLport, slower than libstdc++ on find in N2271, eastl adapter dropped from the current suite, 2019 toolchain unconfirmed.

tier_reason: No benchmark_url and no published numbers: the README makes no speed claim beyond 'contiguous memory layouts for optimal cache performance', and test/Performance/unordered_map/unordered_map/unordered_map.cpp is a Windows-only harness that prints std and ETL milliseconds but ships no results, flags or hardware. A further WebSearch found no independent ETL-vs-std timing.

corrections.caveats: Tier D: the project does not claim to be faster than the std containers; its stated goals are determinism and heap-free operation for embedded targets. A Windows-only timing harness exists (QueryPerformanceCounter, Visual Studio project): https://github.com/ETLCPP/etl/blob/master/test/Performance/unordered_map/unordered_map/unordered_map.cpp, but it ships no results, flags or hardware, so running it is the way to get tier A evidence. Where ETL is faster, the likely cause is avoided heap allocation, which a fixed-capacity container gets by construction; a std::vector with reserve() or a pooled allocator would narrow the gap. Searched the README, docs/containers, docs/blog and test/Performance, plus two WebSearch queries for independent ETL-vs-std timings; none found. The etlcpp.com site was not opened. The harness itself is crude: the std::unordered_map loop runs first in the same process, the etl::unordered_map is a 10,000,000-capacity static global (its storage is pre-sized, while the std map rehashes as it grows in round one), the insert results are unused, and there is a single timing per container with no repetitions. The README states ETL is 'not intended as a full replacement' for the STL. A third WebSearch query (verifier) also found no ETL-vs-std benchmark.

notes: Record accurate; harness code matches (16 rounds of insert-then-erase of 10M sequential uint64_t->uint16_t keys, QueryPerformanceCounter). No numbers anywhere; tier D stays; notable (3.1k stars, 549 forks, last commit 2026-10-04, MIT). Shortcoming: no performance claim or published measurement; determinism, not speed, is the goal.
